ui_idx_h: Understand Malaysia: 12 topics for new buyers
ui_idx_p: Short guides to the country, its people, daily life and what it means for buying a home here.
p1s1p: Peninsular Malaysia borders Thailand to the north and Singapore to the south. East Malaysia, made up of Sabah and Sarawak, shares the island of Borneo with Indonesia and Brunei. Most people, and most of the property market, are on the peninsula: the Klang Valley around Kuala Lumpur, Penang in the north and Johor in the south.
p1s2p: Malaysia has 13 states and 3 federal territories: Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya and Labuan. Nine states have hereditary rulers, and every five years they choose one of themselves as King (Yang di-Pertuan Agong). The Prime Minister leads the government from Putrajaya. Land is a state matter, which is why the rules for foreign buyers can differ from state to state.
p1s3p: Cars drive on the left. Plugs are the three-pin British type. The currency is the ringgit (RM) and the country calling code is +60. Most states take Saturday and Sunday as the weekend, but a few in the north and east rest on Friday and Saturday, so check before you plan office visits there.
p2s1p: Melaka sits on the Strait of Malacca, one of the busiest sea lanes in the world. Around 1400 it became a sultanate that drew traders from China, India, Arabia and the islands around it. Islam spread through the region with this trade, and the Ming admiral Zheng He called at Melaka on his voyages.
p2s2p: The Portuguese captured Melaka in 1511 and the Dutch took it in 1641. The British founded George Town in Penang in 1786 and Singapore in 1819, and gained Melaka in 1824. Tin mines and rubber estates brought large numbers of workers from China and India. Kuala Lumpur itself began in the mid-1800s as a tin-mining settlement where two rivers meet.
p2s3p: Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957 under its first Prime Minister, Tunku Abdul Rahman. Malaysia was formed in 1963 with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore; Singapore left in 1965. George Town and Melaka were listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008, and Kuala Lumpur's skyline now includes both the Petronas Twin Towers and Merdeka 118.
p3s1p: Bumiputera, meaning Malays and the indigenous peoples such as the Orang Asli on the peninsula and the Iban and Kadazan-Dusun in Borneo, make up about seven in ten citizens. Chinese Malaysians, mostly descended from southern Chinese migrants, are about one in five, and Indian Malaysians, mostly Tamil, are the next largest group. Melaka and Penang are also home to the Peranakan (Baba-Nyonya) community.
p3s2p: About six in ten Malaysians are Muslim. Buddhism is the next largest faith, followed by Christianity and Hinduism, along with Taoism and traditional Chinese beliefs. In older neighbourhoods a mosque, a Chinese temple, a Hindu temple and a church can stand within a few streets of each other.
p3s3p: Take off your shoes before entering a home or a place of worship, and dress modestly when visiting a mosque. Give and receive things with your right hand. Many Muslims do not eat pork or drink alcohol, so restaurants that serve them are usually labelled non-halal.
p4s1p: Malay is written in the Latin alphabet and is easy to read aloud. A few words help with addresses and project names: jalan (road), taman (residential estate), bukit (hill), sungai (river), bandar (town), pusat (centre) and terima kasih (thank you).
p4s2p: English is used every day in business, banking, malls and road signs in the cities, and property documents are commonly in English. Malaysian English borrows words from other local languages, and the friendly 'lah' at the end of a sentence is famous.
p4s3p: Mandarin is widely spoken among Chinese Malaysians and in business. Cantonese is common in Kuala Lumpur and Hokkien in Penang. The national school system includes Chinese-medium and Tamil-medium primary schools, and there are daily newspapers in Malay, English, Chinese and Tamil.
p5s1p: Start with nasi lemak: rice cooked in coconut milk with sambal, anchovies, peanuts and egg. Then try roti canai with dhal, char kway teow, satay, Penang assam laksa, banana leaf rice and bak kut teh from Klang. Each state has its own favourites.
p5s2p: Malaysians eat out often. Hawker centres, kopitiam (coffee shops) and food courts serve cheap, quick meals, and mamak stalls run by Indian Muslims stay open late, some all night. Food delivery apps are widely used in the cities.
p5s3p: Many restaurants are halal-certified by JAKIM, the Islamic development department. Chinese restaurants may serve pork and are labelled non-halal. Vegetarians do well at Indian restaurants and Chinese Buddhist vegetarian eateries.
p6s1p: Hari Raya Aidilfitri marks the end of Ramadan, and Hari Raya Haji follows about two months later. Chinese New Year, Deepavali, Christmas and Wesak Day are national holidays too. Thaipusam draws huge crowds to Batu Caves, and Sabah and Sarawak celebrate their harvest festivals, Kaamatan and Gawai, in May and June.
p6s2p: At festival time many families hold an open house and welcome friends and neighbours of every background. During Ramadan, evening bazaars sell food for breaking the fast, and they are worth a visit even if you are not fasting.
p6s3p: Muslim holidays follow the Islamic lunar calendar and come about 11 days earlier each year. Chinese New Year follows the Chinese calendar and falls in January or February. States also have their own holidays, such as the ruler's birthday, so check the official list for the year.
p7s1p: KL Sentral links the LRT, MRT, Monorail, KTM Komuter and the airport trains. The Kelana Jaya and Ampang lines are the older LRT lines, the MRT Kajang and Putrajaya lines run across the city, and newer lines such as LRT3 and the planned MRT3 Circle Line will reach more suburbs.
p7s2p: KTM's ETS electric trains run up and down the west coast, linking Kuala Lumpur with Ipoh, Butterworth for Penang and other towns. Budget flights connect Kuala Lumpur with Penang, Johor Bahru, Kota Kinabalu and Kuching. In the south, the RTS Link rail line between Johor Bahru and Woodlands in Singapore is being built.
p7s3p: Tolled highways link the suburbs and the North–South Expressway runs the length of the peninsula. Tolls, parking and trains can be paid with a Touch 'n Go card or e-wallet. Ride-hailing apps such as Grab are cheap and easy to use.
p8k1v: Pavilion, The Exchange TRX, Mid Valley
p8s1p: In a hot, rainy climate, malls are where people shop, eat, see films and meet friends. Many have supermarkets, clinics, banks and gyms under one roof, and some are linked to train stations by covered walkways.
p8s2p: In Kuala Lumpur, Pavilion and The Exchange TRX are the big names around Bukit Bintang and the Tun Razak Exchange, with Mid Valley Megamall and The Gardens to the south and Pavilion Bukit Jalil further out. Sunway Pyramid and 1 Utama are well known in Selangor, Gurney Plaza in Penang and Mid Valley Southkey in Johor Bahru.
p8s3p: For daily needs there are supermarkets such as AEON, Lotus's, Jaya Grocer and Village Grocer, plus small convenience shops on almost every street. Pasar malam night markets set up in each neighbourhood on a fixed day of the week.
p9s1p: See the Petronas Twin Towers and the park below them, climb the 272 steps of Batu Caves, visit Thean Hou Temple and Merdeka Square, and walk Petaling Street and Kampung Baru. Genting Highlands, cool and green, is about an hour's drive away, and Putrajaya about half an hour.
p9s2p: George Town in Penang is known for its shophouses, clan houses, street art and food. Melaka has the Dutch-era Stadthuys, the ruins of A Famosa and Jonker Street. Ipoh's old town, between the two, is famous for its white coffee.
p9s3p: Langkawi is a group of 99 islands with beaches and a cable car. Redang, Perhentian and Tioman are known for clear water. Cameron Highlands has tea estates, Taman Negara is one of the oldest rainforests in the world, and Sabah offers Mount Kinabalu, the orangutans of Sepilok and diving at Sipadan.
p10s1p: Local food, public transport and petrol cost relatively little compared with many cities in the region. Imported goods, alcohol and cars cost more, cars because of import and excise duties. International school fees are often a family's biggest cost.
p10s2p: Strata homes pay a monthly maintenance fee and a sinking fund to the management. Quit rent (cukai tanah) is paid yearly to the state land office, and assessment tax (cukai pintu) to the local council, usually twice a year. Add electricity, water and internet.
p10s3p: Cards, DuitNow QR codes and e-wallets such as Touch 'n Go eWallet are widely accepted, but small stalls may take cash only. A local bank account makes it easier to pay bills and fees.
p11s1p: Families can choose British (IGCSE and A-Level), American, Australian or IB programmes. Many schools cluster in Mont Kiara, Desa ParkCity, Bangsar, Cyberjaya and Setia Alam in the Klang Valley, in Penang, and in EduCity at Iskandar Puteri in Johor.
p11s2p: Besides public universities such as Universiti Malaya, several foreign universities run full campuses here: Monash in Bandar Sunway, the University of Nottingham in Semenyih, Xiamen University Malaysia in Sepang and Heriot-Watt in Putrajaya. Many students come from across Asia and the Middle East.
p11s3p: Public hospitals and clinics serve everyone, with lower fees for citizens. Private hospitals are widely used, doctors usually speak English, and many visitors come for treatment from abroad. Health insurance is a good idea for foreigners. In an emergency, call 999.
p12s1p: Many nationalities can visit without a visa, but the allowed length of stay depends on your passport. Most foreign visitors must also fill in the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card online before arriving. Rules change, so check the Immigration Department of Malaysia before you travel.
p12s2p: For long stays there is the Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) programme, and Sarawak and Sabah run their own versions. Others come on work passes, student passes or the DE Rantau pass for digital nomads. Our MM2H guide covers the tiers and steps.
p12s3p: It is warm and humid all year. The northeast monsoon brings heavy rain to the east coast and Borneo from about November to March, and afternoon thunderstorms are common everywhere. Malaysia is largely spared typhoons. Day to day it is a safe place to live; take normal care with bags and phones in crowds.
p1s4p: Malaysia is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy. The King, the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, is chosen for five years from among the nine Malay rulers, and the Prime Minister leads the government. The 13 states also have their own governments, and land is a state matter. That is why each state sets its own rules and minimum prices for foreign buyers, and why state consent is part of a foreign purchase.
p1s5h: Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya and the big cities
p1s5p: Kuala Lumpur is the capital and the main business city. Putrajaya, about 25km south, is where most federal ministries sit, next to the tech town of Cyberjaya. Other big centres are George Town in Penang, Johor Bahru across the causeway from Singapore, Ipoh, Melaka, Kota Kinabalu in Sabah and Kuching in Sarawak. Each has its own character, cost of living and property market.
p1s6p: Malaysia is an upper-middle-income economy with a large manufacturing base. Penang is a hub for electronics and semiconductors, Johor is drawing data centres and new industry, and the Klang Valley is the centre for services, finance and retail. Palm oil, oil and gas, and tourism are also important. These jobs are what drive housing demand in each area.
p1s7p: Power is 240V with the UK-style three-pin plug. Cars drive on the left. A prepaid SIM card from a mobile network such as CelcomDigi, Maxis or U Mobile can be bought at the airport or a convenience store with your passport, and mobile data is cheap and fast in the cities. The emergency number is 999. Tap water is treated, but most homes use a filter for drinking.
p2s4p: Around 1400 a prince from Sumatra, Parameswara, founded Melaka on the Strait of Malacca. It grew into one of the busiest ports in Asia, trading spices, textiles and gold, and its rulers embraced Islam. The Melaka Sultanate set many of the customs, court traditions and the language that shaped the Malay world, until the Portuguese captured the city in 1511.
p2s5p: In the 1800s tin mining and later rubber plantations brought rapid growth. Kuala Lumpur began as a tin-mining settlement where the Klang and Gombak rivers meet, and Ipoh grew from the tin of the Kinta Valley. Workers and traders came from southern China and southern India, and many families stayed. This is why Malaysia's towns have Chinese shophouses, Indian temples and Malay villages side by side.
p2s6p: Malaya became independent from Britain on 31 August 1957, celebrated every year as Hari Merdeka. On 16 September 1963 Malaya joined with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore to form Malaysia; Singapore left in 1965. Both dates are national holidays, and Malaysia Day is a reminder that Sabah and Sarawak keep special rights, including their own immigration controls.
p2s7p: Melaka and George Town have been UNESCO World Heritage cities since 2008, with streets of shophouses, clan houses, churches, mosques and temples. In Kuala Lumpur, Merdeka Square, the old railway station and the Masjid Jamek area show the colonial-era city. Many restored shophouses are now cafes, shops and small hotels, and some older homes near these centres are protected, which limits how they can be changed.
p3s4h: Bumiputera and what it means for buyers
p3s4p: Bumiputera, meaning sons of the soil, refers to Malays and the indigenous peoples of Sabah, Sarawak and the peninsula, including the Orang Asli. In new housing projects, a share of units is set aside for Bumiputera buyers, often with a discount, and some land is Malay Reserve Land. Foreigners cannot buy Bumiputera-quota units or Malay Reserve Land, so always check a unit's status before you book.
p3s5p: Family ties are close, and weekends often mean meals with parents, cousins and friends. Neighbours tend to be friendly but private, and in condos the residents' committee and management office run daily life. Food is the easiest way to connect: sharing snacks during a festival, or asking a neighbour for their favourite stall, is a good start.
p3s6h: Visiting homes and places of worship
p3s6p: Take off your shoes before entering a home, and at mosques and most temples. When visiting a mosque, cover your arms and legs; many larger mosques lend robes and headscarves to visitors. Avoid pointing your feet at people or touching someone's head. During Ramadan, eating and drinking in front of Muslim friends who are fasting is best avoided out of courtesy.
p3s7p: A light handshake is common, but some Muslims prefer not to shake hands with the opposite sex; a smile and a hand on the heart is a polite alternative, so let the other person lead. Use your right hand to give and receive things. You will hear honorary titles such as Datuk, Dato' Sri and Tan Sri, awarded by the King and state rulers, and it is polite to use them.
p4s4p: A few words go a long way: terima kasih (thank you), berapa? (how much?), tolong (please, help), jalan (road) and makan (eat). Malaysians also mix languages in one sentence, a style called Manglish, with endings such as 'lah' and words like 'tapau' for takeaway. Most people in the cities switch easily between Malay, English and their home language.
p4s5p: Mandarin is taught in Chinese schools, but many families also speak a southern Chinese dialect at home. Cantonese is common in Kuala Lumpur and Ipoh, Hokkien in Penang and parts of Johor and Melaka, and Hakka, Teochew and Foochow in other towns, especially in Sabah and Sarawak. Chinese-speaking buyers will usually find agents, lawyers and bank officers who can explain things in Mandarin or Cantonese.
p4s6h: Malay words you will see when buying
p4s6p: Property papers often use Malay terms. Geran is a land title, hakmilik strata a strata title, cukai tanah is quit rent and cukai pintu is assessment tax. Pemaju means developer, rumah teres a terrace house, and Perjanjian Jual Beli is the Sale and Purchase Agreement. Your lawyer explains the documents, but knowing these words makes the process much less confusing.
p4s7p: Malay is written in the Latin alphabet and spelled as it sounds, with no tones and simple grammar, so basic phrases come quickly. You may also see Jawi, an Arabic-based script, on mosques, palaces and some signboards, especially in Kelantan and Terengganu. Short courses are offered by language centres and universities, and many apps teach the basics.
p5s4p: Many Malaysians start the day with nasi lemak, coconut rice with sambal, egg, peanuts and anchovies, or roti canai, a flaky flatbread with curry, and a glass of teh tarik, pulled milk tea. Mamak restaurants, run by Indian Muslim families, serve these from early morning, and some stay open late into the night or around the clock. They are where friends meet to watch football and talk.
p5s5p: Every state has dishes it is proud of. Penang is known for char kway teow and assam laksa, Ipoh for white coffee and bean sprout chicken, and Melaka for chicken rice balls and Nyonya cooking, which mixes Chinese and Malay flavours. Kelantan and Terengganu are known for nasi kerabu and keropok lekor, and Sarawak for Sarawak laksa and kolo mee. Food trips between cities are a national hobby.
p5s6p: Supermarkets such as AEON, Lotus's, Jaya Grocer and Village Grocer stock local and imported food, while small chains like 99 Speedmart and KK Mart are on almost every corner. Wet markets sell fresh fish, meat and vegetables early in the morning and are usually cheaper. Food delivery through apps such as GrabFood and foodpanda is fast and widely used, even late at night.
p5s7p: Malaysia is famous for durian, the strong-smelling king of fruits, with varieties such as Musang King. The main season usually runs around the middle of the year, with a smaller one near the end of the year, depending on the weather. Many hotels, trains and condos do not allow durian inside, so check the house rules. Mangosteen, rambutan, mango and papaya are easy to find all year.
p6s4p: During Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset for a month. Ramadan bazaars open in the late afternoon with food stalls of every kind, and restaurants fill up at the breaking of the fast. Hari Raya Aidilfitri marks the end of the month, when many people return to their home towns, so highways are busy and cities feel quiet. Hari Raya Haji follows about two months later.
p6s5p: Chinese New Year is celebrated for 15 days, with lion dances, mandarin oranges, red packets and family reunion dinners, ending with Chap Goh Mei. Many Chinese-run shops close for several days. Later in the year come the Mid-Autumn Festival with mooncakes and lanterns, and the Hungry Ghost month, when some buyers prefer not to sign or move house, so developers and agents often plan around it.
p6s6p: Deepavali, the Hindu festival of lights, brings oil lamps, kolam floor art and open houses. At Thaipusam, large crowds walk to the Batu Caves temple near Kuala Lumpur and to the hilltop temple in Penang. Christmas is a public holiday, and malls put up big decorations. Wesak Day marks the Buddha's birth, while Sarawak celebrates Gawai and Sabah celebrates Kaamatan, both harvest festivals.
p6s7p: Most states have Saturday and Sunday weekends, but Kelantan, Terengganu and Kedah take Friday and Saturday off. Each state also has its own holidays, such as the ruler's birthday. Banks, land offices and lawyers close on public holidays, and long festive breaks can slow down loan approvals, signings and key handovers, so build in extra time when a purchase falls near a big festival.
p7s4p: Rapid KL runs the LRT, MRT, Monorail and BRT lines plus city and feeder buses, and many MRT stations have feeder buses to nearby housing areas. KTM Komuter trains link Kuala Lumpur with Klang, Port Klang, Seremban and Rawang. Fares are paid by tapping a Touch 'n Go card or a Rapid KL card, and monthly passes help regular commuters save. Trains run from early morning until around midnight.
p7s5p: KLIA, the main international airport, is about 50km south of the city. The KLIA Ekspres train reaches KL Sentral in around half an hour, and KLIA Transit stops at stations along the way. Other airports with international flights include Penang, Senai near Johor Bahru, Kota Kinabalu and Kuching, and Subang near Kuala Lumpur handles some regional flights. Airlines such as Malaysia Airlines, AirAsia and Batik Air connect the main cities several times a day.
p7s6h: Getting around Penang and Johor Bahru
p7s6p: Penang Island is linked to the mainland by two bridges and a ferry, and Rapid Penang buses cover the island; an LRT line is being built. In Johor Bahru, most people drive, and the Causeway and the Second Link carry traffic to Singapore. The KTM Shuttle Tebrau train runs across the Causeway today, and the RTS Link from Bukit Chagar to Woodlands North is targeted to open in early 2027.
p7s7p: Visitors can usually drive with their home licence together with an International Driving Permit, and long-term residents can apply to convert to a Malaysian licence. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, so many people plan their home around their commute. Most highways and parking now take Touch 'n Go, RFID tags or e-wallets rather than cash, and the subsidised RON95 petrol price is for Malaysian citizens, so foreigners pay the regular price.
p8s4p: Many newer condos are built next to, above or with a covered link to a mall or a rail station. For residents this means groceries, clinics, gyms and food within a short walk, which is a big plus in the hot, rainy climate. For owners, a direct link to a mall or station is one of the features tenants look for, so it helps a unit stay in demand.
p8s5p: Outside the malls, pasar malam night markets set up once or twice a week in most neighbourhoods, selling street food, fruit, clothes and household goods. Morning wet markets are the place for fresh produce and local breakfast. Living near a good market is something many local families value, and it gives a neighbourhood much of its character.
p8s6h: Opening hours, sales and online shopping
p8s6p: Most malls open from about 10am to 10pm every day, including weekends and many public holidays. Big sales come around mid-year, the year-end holidays and major festivals. Online shopping on platforms such as Shopee, Lazada and TikTok Shop is very popular, and parcels to the cities usually arrive within a few days; most condos have a guardhouse or parcel lockers to receive them.
p9s4p: When the city feels too hot, people head for the hills. Cameron Highlands, about three to four hours from Kuala Lumpur, is known for tea estates, strawberry farms and cool air. Genting Highlands, under an hour away, has a casino, theme parks and an outlet mall, and Fraser's Hill is a quiet colonial-era retreat for walks and birdwatching.
p9s5p: Langkawi, a duty-free island off Kedah, has beaches, cable cars and mangrove tours. On the east coast, the Perhentian, Redang and Tioman islands have clear water for snorkelling, but many resorts close during the northeast monsoon, roughly November to February. Off Sabah, Sipadan and Mabul are among the world's best-known dive sites, with a daily limit on Sipadan permits.
p9s6p: In Sabah, Mount Kinabalu is the highest peak in Malaysia and a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the Sepilok centre cares for orphaned orangutans. In Sarawak, Gunung Mulu National Park, also on the UNESCO list, has some of the largest caves in the world, and Semenggoh near Kuching lets visitors see semi-wild orangutans. Remember that Sabah and Sarawak run their own immigration checks, even for Malaysians from the peninsula.
p9s7h: Easy weekend trips from Kuala Lumpur
p9s7p: Melaka is about two hours by road for heritage streets and Nyonya food, and Ipoh about two and a half hours by ETS train for caves, temples and cafes. Closer to home, Putrajaya has lakes and grand architecture, Kuala Selangor is known for its fireflies, and Port Dickson has the nearest beaches to the capital. Short trips like these are a big part of life here.
p10s4p: The currency is the Malaysian ringgit (RM or MYR), divided into 100 sen. Notes come in RM1, RM5, RM10, RM20, RM50 and RM100, and coins in 5, 10, 20 and 50 sen. Cash bills are rounded to the nearest 5 sen. Licensed money changers in malls usually give better rates than airports, and you will need your passport to change money. You can switch the prices on this site to your own currency at the top of the page.
p10s5p: The Touch 'n Go card is a prepaid card for trains, buses, highway tolls and parking, sold and topped up at convenience stores and stations. The Touch 'n Go eWallet app is used to pay at shops and stalls by QR code, pay bills and top up; foreigners can usually register with a passport, although some features may be limited. DuitNow QR codes, shown at most counters, accept payments from Malaysian bank apps and e-wallets such as Touch 'n Go eWallet, GrabPay, Boost and ShopeePay.
p10s6h: Bank accounts and paying for a home
p10s6p: Each bank sets its own rules for foreigners, but you will usually need your passport, a valid pass or visa and proof of address, and some banks also ask for a reference or a minimum deposit. Property payments go to the developer's project account or, for a subsale, through the lawyers' client accounts, never to an agent personally. When you send money from overseas, keep the bank records, as the lawyers and the bank will ask for them.
p10s7p: Prices in shops usually include tax. Malaysia charges a sales tax of 5% or 10% on many goods and a service tax on many services, which appears on bills at restaurants, hotels and some other businesses. Many restaurants also add a 10% service charge. Tipping is not expected, although rounding up for good service is appreciated.
p10s8p: Electricity comes from TNB on the peninsula, SESB in Sabah and SEB in Sarawak, and water from each state's water company, such as Air Selangor. Home fibre broadband from providers such as Unifi, Maxis, TIME and CelcomDigi is widely available in condos. New owners and tenants usually pay a deposit when opening utility accounts, and most bills can be paid in a banking app or e-wallet.
p11s4p: International schools in Malaysia teach British, American, Australian, Canadian or International Baccalaureate programmes, and many families choose a home within a short drive of the school. Clusters are found around Mont Kiara, Damansara and Bangsar, Cyberjaya and Putrajaya, Iskandar Puteri's EduCity in Johor, and Penang. Popular schools can have waiting lists, so apply early and visit before you buy.
p11s5p: Public hospitals and clinics are very affordable for Malaysians, while foreigners pay higher fees there. Many expatriates use private hospitals, which are modern, have short waiting times and draw medical tourists from across the region. Costs are reasonable by international standards but can add up, so good health insurance is strongly recommended; MM2H applicants are also required to have medical cover.
p11s6p: For minor illnesses, most people visit a GP clinic, found in almost every row of shops, and some open 24 hours. Pharmacy chains such as Watsons, Guardian and Caring sell everyday medicines, and pharmacists can advise on simple problems. Dental and eye care are good value. Keep a list of the nearest clinic and hospital emergency department when you choose where to live.
p11s7p: Pre-schools, called tadika, take children from about four years old, and there are international, Montessori, Chinese-language and Islamic options. Swimming, music, sports, language and coding classes are easy to find, often inside malls or neighbourhood shop lots. Many condos also have pools, playgrounds and courts, which is one reason families like them.
p12s4p: Malaysia has two main monsoon seasons. The southwest monsoon, roughly May to September, is relatively drier on the west coast. The northeast monsoon, roughly November to March, brings heavy rain to the east coast, Sabah and Sarawak, and is when east coast islands quieten down. Between them, around April and October, afternoon thunderstorms are common. Sunrise and sunset stay near 7am and 7pm all year.
p12s5p: Heavy downpours can cause flash floods in some low-lying urban spots, and parts of the east coast see seasonal floods most years. Before you buy, ask about the area's flood history and check the developer's drainage plans. In some dry spells, smoke from regional land and forest fires causes haze; the Department of Environment publishes the air pollutant index online, and an air purifier helps on bad days.
p12s6p: Dengue fever, spread by mosquitoes, is common in Malaysia, so use repellent, fix window screens and make sure no water collects in pots or drains around your home. Drink filtered or bottled water and stay hydrated in the heat. Petty crime such as bag snatching happens in busy areas, so keep bags on the side away from the road. Most condos have guards, access cards and CCTV.
p12s7p: Call 999 for police and ambulance, and 994 for the fire and rescue service; from a mobile phone, 112 also connects to emergency services. Private hospitals run their own ambulance services and 24-hour emergency departments. Save the numbers of your condo's management office and guardhouse, which can help quickly with problems in the building.
